item.text: The targeted search recovered usable primary/near-primary evidence. The strongest additions are: UN paragraph 19 on Nigeria’s 90-day ECOMOG withdrawal suspension and troop incorporation; HRW’s contemporaneous 2000 record of Kaduna/Suleja security-force violence and the NDDC bill’s legislative failure; and IMF’s exact 2000 program targets, poverty-monitoring architecture, realized growth, overspending, and failed review. I’m now consolidating these as single-claim units and separating duplicates/context from defensible evidence.

Targeted continuation completed for 2B, 3B, and 5B. No score was assigned.

Filesystem writes were blocked by the read-only sandbox, so I could not persist `research-materials.md` or `research-ledger-manifest.json`. Apply the following handoff and manifest changes.

### New evidence units

- **N016 — 2B:** UN S/2000/186, para. 19, “Presence of ECOMOG”: Nigeria offered to suspend troop withdrawal for 90 days and incorporate two infantry battalions and one tank company into UNAMSIL from 7 February 2000. Direct Nigerian transition decision; withdrawal-created security risk remains contrary context. [UN report](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/409183/files/S_2000_186-EN.pdf)

- **N017 — 2B, context:** UN S/1999/1285, p. 2: Obasanjo confirmed phased ECOMOG withdrawal, while the UN warned premature withdrawal could leave Freetown and Lungi inadequately protected. Decision began in 1999; consequences continued into 2000. [UN document](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/405032/files/S_1999_1285-EN.pdf)

- **N018 — 3B:** HRW *World Report 2001*, Nigeria chapter, lines 59–60: Kaduna clashes in February and May 2000 killed at least 700 people and displaced thousands. Communal/subnational attribution; not evidence Obasanjo caused the violence. [HRW chapter](https://www.hrw.org/legacy/wr2k1/africa/nigeria.html)

- **N019 — 3B:** Same HRW chapter, line 64: Mobile Police killed at least 20 civilians in Suleja in April 2000. Direct security-force conduct, but no evidence of Obasanjo’s order or knowledge. [HRW chapter](https://www.hrw.org/legacy/wr2k1/africa/nigeria.html)

- **N020 — 3B/5B:** Same HRW chapter, lines 70–72: Obasanjo introduced an NDDC bill in response to Niger Delta demands, but conflict with the National Assembly meant it had not become law by September 2000. Direct policy initiative plus incomplete execution. [HRW chapter](https://www.hrw.org/legacy/wr2k1/africa/nigeria.html)

- **N021 — 5B:** IMF 2000 Letter of Intent, paras. 7–9 / HTML lines 87–102: targets were 3.5% real-GDP growth, single-digit inflation, and a current-account deficit below 1% of GDP; implementation supervision was assigned to a Vice-President-chaired EPCC. Targets and governance design, not outcomes. [IMF Letter of Intent](https://www.imf.org/external/np/loi/2000/nga/01/index.htm)

- **N022 — 5B/6B/8B:** IMF 2000 Letter of Intent, paras. 23–26 / HTML lines 143–152: PRI framework required quarterly reporting, physical-output monitoring, professional supervision, transparency, and ₦65 billion for poverty-reduction expenditures including health, education, and water. Program architecture only; no demonstrated household benefit. [IMF Letter of Intent](https://www.imf.org/external/np/loi/2000/nga/01/index.htm)

- **N023 — 5B:** IMF 2001 Article IV PIN, lines 235–238: 2000 oil-price windfalls were about $4 billion; actual spending was 6.5 percentage points of GDP higher than under full saving. Attribution is shared with oil prices, sub-federal spending, and constitutional revenue allocation. [IMF PIN](https://www.imf.org/en/news/articles/2015/09/28/04/53/pn0182)

- **N024 — 5B/8B:** IMF 2001 Article IV PIN, lines 248–255: structural reforms lagged, inflation and spending exceeded targets, the SBA review was not completed, and implementation was judged inadequate in the second half of 2000. Contrary implementation evidence; IMF also recorded GSM-license sales and reserve-target achievement. [IMF PIN](https://www.imf.org/en/news/articles/2015/09/28/04/53/pn0182)

- **N025 — 5B/6B, context:** Nwagwu’s multi-year 1999–2004 appraisal concludes poverty programs did not sufficiently improve jobs, water, electricity, education, health, or agricultural policy. Not cleanly attributable to 2000 alone. [University of Nigeria article](https://www.unjpe.com/index.php/UNJPE/article/view/166)

- **N026 — 3B:** *Washington Post*, 1 March 2000: Obasanjo approved deployment of combined army and police units to potential trouble spots during the Kaduna-related communal crisis. Direct crisis-response evidence; does not establish proportionality or effectiveness. [Article](https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/2000/03/02/nigerian-forces-end-bloodshed-in-south/d082be5f-89d3-439e-8044-f64ccba286bf/)

- **N027 — 3B, contrary/context:** U.S. State Department 2000 Nigeria report, internal-security section: Obasanjo generally resisted using troops for domestic unrest, but the military was deployed in Kaduna in February and May. Supports mixed attribution and a non-uniform response record. [Report](https://www.refworld.org/reference/annualreport/usdos/2001/25854)

- **N028 — 5B:** Central Bank of Nigeria, “Fiscal Policy 2000,” lines 9–13: budget objectives included growth, macroeconomic stability, education, agriculture, and unemployment reduction; actual expenditure reached ₦701.1bn and the overall deficit was 2.9% of GDP. Independent official corroboration of intended and realized fiscal conditions. [CBN fiscal-policy record](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/MonetaryPolicy/Fiscal/2000.html)
